questions.question: What is the opposite of "ancient"?
questions.fact: "Modern" comes from the Latin "modo", meaning "just now".

questions.question: How many letters are in the English alphabet?
questions.fact: "The quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog" uses all 26 letters of the English alphabet.

questions.question: How many letters does the Spanish alphabet have, including ñ?
questions.fact: Spain's language academy officially dropped "ch" and "ll" as separate letters in 2010, leaving 27, with ñ the only extra one.

questions.question: What do we call a word that means the same as another?
questions.fact: English has lots of synonyms because it borrowed words from both French and old Germanic languages.

questions.question: What do we call a word with the opposite meaning?
questions.fact: The opposite of an antonym is a synonym, so "synonym" and "antonym" are antonyms of each other.

questions.question: What does the Italian word "ciao" mean?
questions.fact: "Ciao" comes from the Venetian "s'ciavo", meaning "your servant".

questions.question: In which language is "danke" thank you?
questions.fact: German nouns always start with a capital letter, like "Danke für den Kaffee".

questions.question: How do you say "thank you" in Japanese?
questions.fact: Japanese uses three writing systems at once: hiragana, katakana and kanji.

questions.question: Which language is spoken in Brazil?
questions.fact: Brazil has more Portuguese speakers than Portugal, about 20 times more people.

questions.question: What is the official language of Austria?
questions.fact: Austrian German has its own words: a tomato is "Paradeiser" and January can be "Jänner".

questions.question: What does "bon appétit" mean?
questions.fact: French speakers say "bon appétit" before eating; in Spain you'll hear "¡que aproveche!".

questions.question: A word that reads the same backwards, like "level", is a…
questions.fact: One of the longest palindromes in English is "A man, a plan, a canal: Panama!"

questions.question: Turning "listen" into "silent" by swapping letters makes an…
questions.fact: "Dormitory" is an anagram of "dirty room", and "astronomer" of "moon starer".

questions.question: A word made from first letters, like NASA, is called an…
questions.fact: "Laser" and "scuba" started as acronyms but are now used as normal words.

questions.question: What does "ASAP" stand for?
questions.fact: ASAP is thought to have started in the US Army in the 1950s before spreading into everyday office talk.

questions.question: What does "RSVP" on an invitation ask you to do?
questions.fact: RSVP stands for "Répondez s'il vous plaît", French for "please reply".

questions.question: "RSVP" comes from which language?
questions.fact: English took lots of polite and formal words from French after the Normans conquered England in 1066.

questions.question: What is the plural of "mouse" (the animal)?
questions.fact: The plural of computer "mouse" can be "mice" or "mouses"; both are used.

questions.question: The famous 45-letter English word is a disease of which body part?
questions.fact: That 45-letter word, pneumonoultramicroscopicsilicovolcanoconiosis, was invented in the 1930s on purpose to be extra long.

questions.question: What is the most common letter in English?
questions.fact: E is the most common letter in English, which is why it's worth just 1 point in Scrabble.

questions.question: Which Spanish word is used in English for an afternoon nap?
questions.fact: "Siesta" comes from the Latin "sexta hora", the sixth hour after dawn: midday.

questions.question: The word "chocolate" comes originally from which language?
questions.fact: The Aztec word was "xocolatl", for a bitter cocoa drink. Spanish explorers brought it to Europe.

questions.question: What does "déjà vu" literally mean?
questions.fact: The opposite feeling, when something familiar suddenly seems strange, is called "jamais vu", "never seen".

questions.question: What is a haiku?
questions.fact: One of the most famous haiku is by Matsuo Bashō, about a frog jumping into an old pond.

questions.question: How many syllables does a traditional haiku have?
questions.fact: A traditional haiku has three lines of 5, 7 and 5 syllables.

questions.question: What does the prefix "bi-" mean, as in bicycle?
questions.fact: "Bi-" comes from Latin. Greek uses "di-" for two instead, as in carbon "dioxide": two oxygen atoms.

questions.question: What does "omni-" mean, as in omnivore?
questions.fact: "Omni" means all in Latin. An "omnibus" (bus) was originally "for all".

questions.question: How do you say "thank you" in Catalan?
questions.fact: Catalan is spoken by around 10 million people in Catalonia, Valencia, the Balearic Islands, Andorra and parts of France and Italy.

questions.question: Which language is spoken alongside Spanish in the Basque Country?
questions.fact: Basque is spoken by around 750,000 people. "Kaixo" means hello and "eskerrik asko" means thank you.

questions.question: Which language of Spain and France is not related to any other known language?
questions.fact: Basque is a "language isolate". It's thought to have been spoken in the region before Latin and its relatives arrived.

questions.question: What are homophones?
options: Words that sound the same but mean different things
questions.fact: "Their", "there" and "they're" are classic English homophones that trip up even native speakers.

questions.question: What does "carpe diem" mean?
questions.fact: "Carpe diem" comes from the Roman poet Horace. It was made famous again by the film "Dead Poets Society".

questions.question: What does "et cetera" (etc.) mean?
questions.fact: The "&" symbol started life as a joined-up way of writing "et", Latin for "and".

questions.question: What does "e.g." mean?
questions.fact: "E.g." is short for the Latin "exempli gratia", "for the sake of example".

questions.question: What does "i.e." mean?
questions.fact: "I.e." is short for the Latin "id est", meaning "that is".

questions.question: A word that imitates a sound, like "buzz", is called…
questions.fact: Onomatopoeia changes by language: a Spanish rooster says "quiquiriquí" and a Spanish dog says "guau".

questions.question: "She sells seashells" repeats the same starting sound. That is called…
questions.fact: Alliteration is popular in brand names like Coca-Cola, PayPal and Dunkin' Donuts.

questions.question: A comparison using "like" or "as" is a…
questions.fact: "As brave as a lion" is a simile; "He is a lion" is a metaphor.

questions.question: "I've told you a million times!" is an example of…
questions.fact: "Hyperbole" comes from Greek and means "throwing beyond".

questions.question: Counting native and second-language speakers, which language is spoken most worldwide?
questions.fact: English has around 1.5 billion speakers, but most of them learned it as a second language.

questions.question: Which country has the most Spanish speakers?
questions.fact: Mexico has over 120 million Spanish speakers, more than twice as many as Spain.

questions.question: What is Esperanto?
options: A language invented to be international
questions.fact: Esperanto was created in 1887 by L. L. Zamenhof. Its name means "one who hopes".

questions.question: What does the German word "Kindergarten" literally mean?
questions.fact: Friedrich Fröbel opened the first kindergarten in Germany in 1837 and invented the name.

questions.question: The English word "hurricane" came through Spanish from which word?
questions.fact: "Huracán" comes from the Taíno people of the Caribbean, possibly from the name of a storm god.

questions.question: What does "sobremesa" mean in Spain?
options: Chatting at the table after a meal
questions.fact: "Sobremesa" has no direct English translation. In Spain, it can easily last longer than the meal itself!

questions.question: What is "guiri" Spanish slang for?
questions.fact: Nobody is completely sure where "guiri" comes from. It's usually playful rather than rude.

questions.question: What does "vale" usually mean in Spain?
questions.fact: Spaniards often say "vale" many times in one conversation, as "OK", "fine" or "got it".

questions.question: What do you say when toasting in Spanish?
questions.fact: When toasting in Spain, people traditionally look each other in the eye. Some say it's bad luck not to.

questions.question: What is the past tense of "go"?
questions.fact: "Went" originally belonged to another verb, "wend", and got borrowed by "go" centuries ago.

questions.question: Which part of speech describes a noun, like "blue" in "blue car"?
questions.fact: In English, adjectives usually come before the noun ("blue car"); in Spanish, usually after ("coche azul").

questions.question: What is a word like "quickly", which describes a verb, called?
questions.fact: Many English adverbs end in "-ly", just as many Spanish ones end in "-mente", like "rápidamente".

questions.question: What does the German word "Wanderlust" mean?
questions.fact: German loves long compound words, like "Handschuh" (glove), literally a "hand shoe".

questions.question: The Danish word "hygge" describes…
questions.fact: Denmark often ranks among the happiest countries in the world. Candles, blankets and good company are classic "hygge".

questions.question: In French, what is a "pamplemousse"?
questions.fact: "Pamplemousse" comes from old Dutch words meaning roughly "swollen lemon".

questions.question: What is "Schadenfreude"?
options: Joy at someone else's bad luck
questions.fact: "Schadenfreude" combines "Schaden" (harm) and "Freude" (joy).

questions.question: How do you say "I love you" in French?
questions.fact: In Spanish, "te quiero" is common between partners and family, while "te amo" sounds more intense.

questions.question: "Ti amo" is "I love you" in which language?
questions.fact: Italian has several words for love: "ti voglio bene" is used for friends and family, "ti amo" for a partner.

questions.question: What is the "&" sign called?
questions.fact: "Ampersand" comes from children reciting the alphabet and ending with "and per se and".

questions.question: What is the wavy line on top of ñ called?
questions.fact: The ñ began as a small "n" written above another "n" to save space in old manuscripts.

questions.question: What is the "@" symbol called in Spanish?
questions.fact: "Arroba" was originally a unit of weight in Spain, about 11.5 kg.

questions.question: What do you call the "#" symbol in Spanish?
questions.fact: "Almohadilla" means "little cushion" in Spanish, maybe because the # looks like a padded cushion.
